The toga is a draped woolen garment worn by male Roman citizens as the formal dress of state, consisting of a large piece of cloth often six yards or more wrapped around the body in a distinctive asymmetrical configuration. More than mere clothing, the toga represented citizenship, legal status, and civic authority, making it one of ancient Rome's most politically significant garments.

Worn exclusively by male citizens, enslaved people, non-citizens, and non-Romans were legally prohibited from wearing togas, making it a marker of political status and belonging. The toga required a specific wrapping technique that took time and skill. Most men employed a slave to drape the toga correctly, as the many folds had to be arranged precisely. The toga pratica was a plain white toga worn as standard civic dress. The toga candida, bright white, was worn by political candidates. The toga picta, embroidered purple, was reserved for generals and emperors.

Worn over a tunica or tunic, the arrangement could indicate social rank, military status, or religious office through variations in color, trim, and draping pattern. The toga was impractical for labor or warfare; the flowing cloth restricted movement, which is why working-class Romans and soldiers preferred simpler tunics and why wearing a toga signaled freedom from manual work. The toga represented Roman identity so strongly that Romans referred to themselves as togati, the toga-wearing people, in contrast to barbarian neighbors who wore pants and shorter garments.

The toga declined in the fourth and fifth centuries of the Common Era as practical tunics and barbarian-influenced clothing replaced it; the garment disappeared from common use by the early medieval period. The toga's significance is bound to the Roman Empire, the political and military system that gave the toga its legal and civic significance. It appears prominently in the contemplations of Marcus Aurelius, the emperor whose philosophical writings contemplate duty and virtue, concepts intimately connected to the toga-wearing citizen ideal. The garment remains the quintessential symbol of ancient Rome, the civilization for which the toga was the quintessential symbol of identity and status.
